passages.where: A man hunted by enemies, wasted by grief and abandoned by friends says to God: my times are in your hands. The site's plain note offers the verse for days when life feels out of control, to be said slowly: in God's hands, not in your boss's, your doctor's or your enemy's. The future is not empty; it is held.

The proverb tells the reader not to boast about tomorrow, for no one knows what a day may bring. The site's note says the chapter opens with sayings on humility about the future. The same truth that humbles the confident person can free the anxious one: no one knows tomorrow, so no one is required to carry it today.

In the wilderness God promises bread from heaven, with an instruction: each day the people are to gather enough for that day. The site's note on the chapter tells how some disobeyed and the hoarded manna rotted, while the double portion before the Sabbath kept, and Israel ate it for forty years. God trained a frightened people to trust him one morning at a time.

A man who has felt God's hand against him, in darkness and chains, calls to mind in the middle of his despair that the LORD's mercies are new every morning. The site's note on the chapter tells how he then resolves to wait for God. The mercy he finds is not stored up for the whole future; it is given new each morning.

Jesus says not to worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. The site's note calls it a proverb of practical realism: Jesus does not promise a trouble-free life; he limits the load to one day at a time. The plain note adds that the passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, which needs care, not blame.

The Teacher says no one understands the work of God, as no one knows the path of the wind, and so tells the reader to sow in the morning and keep working in the evening, for no one knows which will succeed. The site's note says he urges bold, generous action in the face of an uncertain future. Not knowing is a reason to keep sowing, not to freeze.

Against the gods of Babylon, statues that have to be loaded onto weary animals and carried away, the LORD says he declares the end from the beginning and his purpose will stand. The site's note on the chapter sets the two side by side: the idols must be carried, while God carries his people from birth into old age. The future frightens us partly because we cannot see it; it does not frighten him.

The psalm describes a person who does not fear bad news, because his heart is steadfast, trusting in the LORD. The site's plain note says that steadiness does not come from having no trouble; it comes from trust. The psalm does not promise there will be no bad news.

The closing poem of Proverbs praises a woman clothed with strength and honor who can laugh at the days to come. The site's note says her worth lies above all in her fear of the LORD. The site's note on the chapter's hard question adds that the poem is praise, not a performance standard; the confidence it describes rests on the fear of the LORD, which is open to every believer.

Hebrews tells its readers to keep free from the love of money and be content, because God has said he will never leave them or forsake them. The site's plain note says verse 5 is not a promise that God will make anyone rich; it is a call to be content because God will never leave. Whatever the future holds, it will not hold his absence.

misread.taken: Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved is taken as a guarantee: pray over the plan and the future will go as planned, so if it does not, something was wrong with the praying.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says it opens with the densest group of sayings about the LORD in the collection: people make plans, but the LORD weighs hearts, establishes steps and decides outcomes. The note on Proverbs 22 explains what a proverb is: it describes how life usually goes, a true generalization, not a contract. Committing a plan to God is wisdom; it is not a promise that every plan will be fulfilled as we drew it.

whole: Fear of the future rarely has one object. It is the job that might not last, the money that might not stretch, the diagnosis that might come back, the child who might not be all right, the country that seems to be coming apart, the old age that might be lonely. Some of it is reasonable, and some of what we dread will in fact come. The mind runs ahead and lives the worst version in advance, again and again, so that a person suffers things that have not happened and may never happen. Over time it can take the joy out of today and make every plan feel like a wager against disaster. If that fear has grown constant or keeps you from sleeping, it is worth taking to a doctor, and that is not a failure of faith.

Scripture does not pretend the future is safe. It says no one knows what a day may bring, and it shows faithful people losing jobs, health and children. What it refuses is the idea that we must hold the future ourselves. Israel in the wilderness tried to store up manna against tomorrow, and it rotted overnight. Underneath much of our fear is that same instinct: if I can only foresee enough, save enough, plan enough, I will be safe. It is not wrong to plan. Proverbs commends the ant. But planning turns into dread when we treat ourselves as the ones who must guarantee the outcome, and most of us have spent nights doing exactly that.

So the Bible's wisdom is to live one day at a time under a God who holds all the days. My times are in your hands, the psalmist says, and that is a sentence to say slowly when the future presses. Attend to today's work, sow in the morning and in the evening, as the Teacher says, because not knowing which will succeed is no reason to stop. Gather today's bread and trust God for tomorrow's. Make plans and hold them loosely, saying if the Lord wills (James 4:15). Tell someone what you fear, and pray about it plainly. Take the next sensible step that is yours to take, and leave the rest with the one who declares the end from the beginning.

The hope Scripture gives is that the future belongs to God, and God has already said how it ends. His mercies are new every morning, and he will never leave or forsake his people. His purpose will stand. The same Jesus who told his followers not to worry about tomorrow walked toward a cross he could see coming, and rose. Whatever the next years hold, they cannot hold anything that has slipped out of his hands, and they will not hold his absence.
sit: What future are you living in advance right now, and what is the one thing God is asking you to do today?

prayer.lead: A pilgrim's song for the road ahead, sung by a traveler and answered with a blessing. The site's plain note says it does not promise that no harm will ever come; it promises that God keeps the one who trusts him, and it is a blessing to carry out the door.

careLines.text: Lost sleep and heavy thoughts are worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a failure of faith.
